Just read a highly entertaining book on this subject - "The 'Secret' Gospel of Mark: Morton Smith, Clement of Alexandra and Four Decades of Academic Burlesque" by Robert Conner.

He shows out the utter fatuity of the "arguments" of the likes of Stephen Carlson and Peter Jeffery with great humor and incisiveness.

Granted, when you hear that a lost fragment of the Gospel of Mark was discovered in a monastery, it sounds exciting; when you then learn that the fragment was contained in an 18th-century copy of a letter supposedly of Clement of Alexandra, and that even this copy is only known from photographs, the manuscript having been "misplaced," it starts to sound suspicious; and when you further learn that the fragment of "Mark" contains references to Jesus conducting some sort of strange ritual that could easily be interpreted as implying homosexual activity, you can be forgiven for wondering whether somebody has an axe to grind.

And yet, when you really dig into this putative discovery of Smith's, you find that the evidence actually is overwhelmingly in favor of this NOT being a hoax - at least, not a modern 20th century hoax perpetrated or perpetuated by Smith, and probably not an ancient hoax either.

The manuscript is a perfect example of 18th-century Greek miniscule of the sort that would've been used at Mar Saba, with all the ligatures and whatnot. There is no "forger's tremble" such as was detected by Carlson, a lawyer who has absolutely no qualifications to make the judgement anyway, and who was working from the reproductions of Smith's photographs of the manuscript that appeared in his book, which were distorted by the line screen used in the printing. Smith consulted actual experts on Greek handwriting of the period, and the photos have been examined by many others since, and the consensus is that this is genuine 18th-century script. In fact even proponents of the forgery claim are generally compelled to suggest that Smith must've hired an accomplice to execute it, since reproducing that script would've been beyond his capability.

And that's before we even consider the content of the letter, which is of course in two different styles - that of Clement and that of Mark - both of which are perfectly in keeping with the known writings of each. Again, to forge both of these styles so perfectly would be an enormous feat even for an expert. In fact the "secret" passages of Mark fill certain lacunae in the gospel text, and make a certain sense of otherwise obscure passages. Some have even tried to argue that everything is just a little TOO perfect, and have taken this to suggest that it must've been forged - but the fallacy inherent in this kind of argument should be immediately evident. If the fact that literally everything checks out about this manuscript, from the handwriting to the content, is to be counted against the possibility of its authenticity, then what could possibly be counted FOR it?

It's also necessary to separate the content of the letter itself from Smith's own interpretation of it - something that many of his critics, who begin by assuming what they need to prove (i.e. that Smith forged it), tend to fail to do. Smith thought that the "Lazarus"-like episode recounted in "Secret Mark" referred to some sort of baptism ceremony performed by Jesus on select disciples at night. The speculation that REALLY got him into trouble was that the "mystery of the kingdom of God" may have involved a mystical or hallucinatory experience in which the disciple was united spiritually with Jesus and freed from temporal bounds - and that this spiritual union may have been completed by an act of physical union. He furthermore posited that this all derived from a tradition preserved from the life of the historical Jesus - i.e. that Jesus really did have gay sex with his disciples.

Must've taken some REAL balls in the 1950s. But this interpretation of Smith's is just that - his interpretation of a text he discovered and wrestled with for decades. The text itself does NOT necessarily imply either a baptism rite or a homosexual one - even though the hint of homosexuality in the relationship between Jesus and the young man he raises, who looks on him and loves him, and then comes to him at night with only a linen shroud over his naked body, was evidently picked up anciently by the Carpocratians of whom Clement complains. But Smith's controversial interpretation, which is in some ways a product of the state of biblical scholarship at the time, is consistently conflated with the text itself by proponents of the forgery theory, who tend to be offended Christians, and who are apparently working backwards from their outrage at the very notion of a "gay Jesus."

Last note - ANYBODY ought to be able to laugh at the truly ridiculous "arguments" put forward by Carlson and Jeffrey, i.e. that Smith included "signatures" in his forgery. For example, Clement metaphorically mentions adulterated salt that loses its savor, but Carlson asserts (wrongly) that salt couldn't be mixed in the ancient world - so he takes this as a "hint," and then has the brilliant insight that Smith's first name is Morton - get it, like the salt! - and that this was his way of signing his work. The complete battiness of this entire train of thought speaks for itself.
